blocks.prompt: The Tube That Found a Hidden World
blocks.text: A microscope has glass lenses inside it. A lens is a piece of glass that is curved. When light goes through a lens, it bends. The bending makes small things look much bigger. You put a tiny thing on a glass slide. You slide it under the lens. Then you look in the top and turn the knob until the thing is clear. A drop of pond water looks empty. Under a microscope, it is not empty at all. It is full of tiny living things swimming around. They were always there. Your eyes just could not see them.

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Named Cells
blocks.text: In 1665, an English scientist named Robert Hooke cut a very thin slice of cork and put it under his microscope. Cork comes from the bark of a tree. Hooke expected to see something solid. Instead he saw rows and rows of tiny empty boxes, all lined up like a honeycomb. The boxes reminded him of the small plain rooms that monks slept in. Those rooms were called cells. So Hooke called the little boxes cells too, and the name stuck. Every living thing you have ever met is made of cells. You are made of them. So is grass, so is a dog, so is mold on old bread. Nobody knew that until somebody looked through curved glass at a piece of bark. Hooke drew everything he saw and put the drawings in a book called Micrographia. There was a flea in it the size of a page, with hairs and claws and armor. People had been living with fleas their whole lives. They had never once seen one.

blocks.prompt: The Cloth Merchant Who Saw Animals in Water
blocks.text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was not a scientist. He sold cloth in the Dutch town of Delft. Cloth merchants used small magnifying glasses to count the threads in a fabric and check its quality, and somewhere along the way van Leeuwenhoek became obsessed with the glass rather than the cloth. He taught himself to melt glass into tiny beads and grind them into lenses no bigger than a pinhead. His microscopes look nothing like the ones you have seen. Each was a small brass plate with a single lens set in a hole, held right up against the eye. They were awkward and fiddly, and they were also the best in the world. Some magnified nearly 270 times, and nobody else came close for over a century. In the 1670s he began pointing them at ordinary things. Rainwater from a barrel. A drop from a lake. In 1683 he scraped the film from between his own teeth, mixed it with clean water, and looked. He saw things moving. Small living creatures, darting and spinning, more of them in his mouth, he wrote, than there were people in the whole kingdom. He called them animalcules. We call them bacteria and protozoa. He sent letter after letter to the Royal Society in London, written in Dutch, full of careful drawings. At first they did not believe him. No one else could see what he described, because no one else had lenses that good. He never told anyone how he made them. He took the method with him when he died.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A 10x eyepiece over a 40x objective gives 400x
Visible light is 400 to 700 nanometers long
A nanometer is one billionth of a meter
Light microscopes cannot resolve below about 200 nanometers
Electron microscopes steer electrons with magnets

blocks.prompt: The Wall That Light Built
blocks.text: For two hundred years after van Leeuwenhoek, the way to see smaller was obvious: grind better glass. Add a second lens. Polish harder. Then, in 1873, a German physicist named Ernst Abbe worked out the mathematics of what a microscope actually does, and found something nobody wanted to hear. There is a wall, and no amount of better glass will get you past it. The problem is light itself. Light travels as a wave, and a wave cannot describe anything much smaller than its own length. Visible light has a wavelength of roughly 400 to 700 nanometers, a nanometer being one billionth of a meter. Abbe showed that a light microscope therefore cannot separate two points closer together than about 200 nanometers. Below that, everything blurs into everything else. You can magnify a blur as much as you like. It stays a blur. Magnification and resolution are not the same thing, and it was Abbe who made that painfully clear. Two hundred nanometers is small. It is not small enough. A bacterium is about a thousand nanometers across, so bacteria were fine. A virus is often around a hundred nanometers, which meant that for decades scientists knew viruses existed, could filter them, could catch diseases from them, and could not look at one. The way through the wall was not glass. In 1931, Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built a microscope in Berlin that used no light at all. It fired a beam of electrons and steered it with magnets instead of lenses. Electrons, it turns out, also behave like waves, but their wavelength is thousands of times shorter than visible light. A shorter wave draws a finer line. Within a few years, electron microscopes were resolving detail far finer than any glass lens ever could, and in 1939 a virus finally sat in a photograph where anyone could look at it. Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986, fifty five years after building the thing. Max Knoll had died in 1969 and did not share it. The wall Abbe found was real, and it is still there. The lesson was that when a limit is built into the tool, you do not sharpen the tool. You change what the tool is made of.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Tube That Found a Hidden World

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Micrographia, Robert Hooke, 1665
Cells were named after the rooms of monks
Abbe's limit, 1873: about 200 nanometers
Ruska and Knoll built the first electron microscope in 1931
Koch found the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882
Super-resolution microscopy won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

blocks.prompt: The Instrument That Kept Rewriting the World
blocks.text: Every so often a tool arrives that does not just answer questions. It invents them. Before 1600, nobody asked what a drop of pond water was made of, because the question had no possible answer and therefore no point. The microscope did not simply supply the answer. It supplied the question. The instrument itself is almost embarrassingly simple. A lens is a piece of glass with a curved face, and curved glass bends light. Arrange two lenses in a tube so that the second one magnifies the image produced by the first, and their powers multiply: a ten times eyepiece over a forty times objective yields four hundred times. Dutch spectacle makers had assembled something like this by the 1590s. Galileo built one around 1625, and a friend of his named the thing from the Greek words mikros, meaning small, and skopein, meaning to look at. For the first sixty years it was mostly a toy for the wealthy. Then two men used it properly. In 1665 Robert Hooke published Micrographia, a book of drawings so fine that people who had lived alongside fleas their entire lives saw one for the first time, sprawled across a fold-out page in armor. Looking at a shaving of cork, Hooke found rows of tiny empty chambers and, reaching for a comparison, called them cells after the bare rooms of monks. He had named the unit of life without knowing it. A decade later, a cloth merchant in Delft with no university training and no intention of publishing anything ground lenses better than anyone alive and turned them on rainwater, lake water, and the scrapings from his own teeth. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek found them swarming. He reported more creatures in his mouth than there were people in the kingdom, and the Royal Society, unable to replicate him, spent years deciding whether to believe him. It took two more centuries for the consequence to land. If invisible living things are everywhere, then invisible living things might be doing something. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch turned that suspicion into germ theory: Koch identified the bacterium behind anthrax in 1876 and behind tuberculosis in 1882, and put each one under a lens where a skeptic could see it. Handwashing, sterilization, antibiotics, and vaccines all descend from that view down a tube. It is not an exaggeration to say the microscope has saved more lives than any other object made of glass. And then the instrument hit its own ceiling. In 1873 Ernst Abbe proved that light, being a wave roughly 400 to 700 nanometers long, cannot resolve two points closer than about 200 nanometers apart. Not a manufacturing problem. A physics problem. Better glass would change nothing. So in 1931 Ruska and Knoll abandoned light entirely and steered a beam of electrons with magnets, because an electron's wave is thousands of times shorter, and viruses finally became visible. Then in the 1990s and 2000s a handful of physicists did something stranger. Rather than defeat Abbe's limit, they sidestepped it, using fluorescent molecules switched on a few at a time so that each blur could be pinpointed and the pinpoints assembled into a picture. The 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell, and William Moerner for it. Four hundred years, and the pattern has never changed. Someone looks closer than anyone has looked. What they find is not a detail of the world already known. It is a world nobody had thought to ask about.
